main.claim: Open the mic test, allow microphone access, and talk: the level meter moves when your mic picks up your voice. Record a clip of up to 10 seconds and play it back. Free, no app, no sign-up, and nothing is uploaded or saved.

sections.heading: How to test your microphone
sections.body:
Open Mic Test in the browser you use every day. When the page asks, select Allow for the microphone. If you have more than one microphone, open the microphone list and pick the one you want to check. Then speak at your normal volume.

1. Open [Mic Test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/).
2. Select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone.
3. Pick the right microphone from the list.
4. Say a sentence at normal volume and watch the meter.

**The meter moves with your voice.** It also keeps the loudest level reached so far, so you can see whether the mic is loud enough without watching the bar the whole time.

If the test works here, the browser has the microphone and is sending its sound to the page. That is the same connection a website uses when it asks for your mic, so this check is a fair first step before a call or a recording.

sections.heading: What the meter tells you
sections.body:
Speak normally and the bar should rise and fall with your voice. If it stays near zero while you talk, the page is not getting sound from that microphone. Try another microphone in the list, check that the right input is selected in your computer's sound settings, and close any other app that might be using the mic.

If the bar hits the top while you talk quietly, move the mic farther from your mouth or lower the input level in your sound settings. You are looking for a steady reading that rises when you speak and falls when you stop.

sections.heading: Record a clip and play it back
sections.body:
Record up to 10 seconds of your voice, then press play. The clip is what the microphone captured, so it shows how you sound to other people. Your own voice often sounds different in your head than it does on a recording.

Listen for three things. Are your words clear? Is the volume steady? Is there any hiss, crackle, hum or echo? A clean clip with clear words is a good sign for a call. If the clip is muffled, the mic may be covered or too far away. Record again after you fix it and compare the two clips.

sections.heading: What happens to your voice
sections.body:
Mic Test runs in your browser. The recording is not uploaded and is not saved, so when you close the page, the clip goes with it. You do not need an account or an app to use it.

To check your camera in the same way, open [Webcam Test](https://webcam-test.lazur.app/) in the same browser.

pages.description: Record up to 10 seconds with your mic in the browser, then play it back to hear how you sound. Live level meter included. Free, no sign-up needed.
pages.claim: Click Record, speak for up to 10 seconds, then press Play to hear the clip. The playback is exactly what your microphone captured, so you hear how you sound to other people. Free, in your browser, nothing uploaded.

sections.heading: How to play back your mic test
sections.body:
Use this steps list to hear your mic:

1. Open the [mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/playback) and select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone.
2. Pick the microphone you want to check, if you have more than one.
3. Speak a sentence or two at your normal volume.
4. Stop the recording, then press Play to hear it.

Listen for three things. Are your words clear? Is the volume steady? Is there hiss, crackle or echo in the background? Your own voice often sounds different in your head than it does on a recording, so judge the clip, not your memory of how you sounded.

A good playback is one you would be happy to send to a colleague. Keep the clip short and natural, speak in your usual tone, and say a sentence you would say on a call, such as your name and what you work on. Then listen as if you are the other person on the call. If you have to strain to hear a word, the other person probably will too. Fix the cause, then record again. Try once in a quiet room and once with a fan or music on, so you know how much background noise gets through.

sections.heading: Why playback matters
sections.body:
The live meter shows that sound is arriving at the page. Playback shows what that sound is like. Fan noise, keyboard clicks and room echo can show up in a recording even when the meter looks fine. If the clip sounds muffled, the mic may be covered by your hand or a case, or you may be sitting too far from it.

**Playback is the better test for calls**, because it shows what another person would hear, not only whether something is coming in.

sections.heading: If the playback is silent or very quiet
sections.body:
Check that the right microphone is picked in the list. Then check the input settings in your computer's sound settings, and raise the input level if it is low. Close any other app that might be using the mic, such as a call app or a recorder. Record again, then press Play.

If the playback is loud but the meter did not move, the browser may have picked a different input. Choose the microphone again in the list and record a new clip.

sections.heading: Playback on headphones or speakers
sections.body:
Playback uses the speakers or headphones your computer is using right now. If you plan to wear headphones on a call, plug them in before you test, so you hear the clip the way the call will sound.

If you dictate every day, Lazur does this in any app on your Mac. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

faq.q: Can I record a mic test online?
faq.a: Yes. Mic Test records a clip of up to 10 seconds with your microphone, then plays it back so you can listen. Nothing is uploaded or saved, and no account is needed. Record again whenever you change microphones or settings.

faq.q: How do I play back my microphone?
faq.a: Record a short clip in the mic test, stop it, and press Play. The clip plays through the speakers or headphones your computer is using. If you hear nothing, pick the right microphone and check your input settings, then record again.

faq.q: Why does my playback sound quiet?
faq.a: The mic is probably too far away, or its input level is low. Move closer, speak at normal volume, and raise the input level in your computer's sound settings. Then record a new 10-second clip and listen again to compare the two.

pages.description: Hear your own voice through your mic in your browser. Record up to 10 seconds, then play it back. Live level meter included. Free, no app needed.
pages.claim: Mic Test does not play your voice back live while you talk. It records up to 10 seconds, then plays the clip so you hear yourself as the mic picked you up. Free, in your browser, with no app.

sections.heading: How to hear your own voice
sections.body:
Open the mic test, select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone, and pick the mic if you have more than one.

1. Press record.
2. Read a short paragraph out loud for up to 10 seconds.
3. Stop the recording and press Play.

Listen with headphones if you can. Speakers can send sound back into the mic and make the test sound worse than it is.

If you are not sure how your voice sounds, record a second clip with the mic at a different distance. Hold it an arm's length away for one take and a hand's width away for another. Play both back. The clip with the cleaner words and steadier level shows the distance to use. Write that distance down, so you can set it up the same way next time. Repeat the test when you change headsets, rooms, or the spot where your computer sits, because each of those changes what the mic hears.

Keep short notes on each test. Write the date, the headset or mic, the room, and whether the clip sounded clear. After three or four tests, you will see which setup gives the cleanest result, and you can reuse it for your next call without repeating the whole check. Keep the notes next to your headset so they are easy to find.

sections.heading: Live hearing is not part of this test
sections.body: This tool shows the live level while you speak, but it plays your voice back after you record. If you want to hear yourself while you talk, that is usually a setting in your headset or your audio app, not something this test turns on. Use the clip to decide whether your mic is clear enough, then change the setting you need in the app you use for calls.

sections.heading: Why hearing a recording helps
sections.body:
When you hear your recording, you can catch problems you do not notice while talking. Room echo, a hum from a fan and words that cut out when you turn your head all show up in the clip. Record a short test in the same spot and posture you will use on a call, then play it back and listen closely.

**Listen to the clip twice.** The first time, check the words. The second time, check the background.

sections.heading: Hearing yourself on a call
sections.body: Apps such as Zoom and Discord have their own mic checks and input settings. Use this test to confirm that your mic works and is loud enough. Then use the app's own test to confirm it uses the same mic. For Zoom, the steps are in its [audio settings guide](https://support.zoom.com/hc/en/article?id=zm_kb&sysparm_article=KB0062765).

faq.q: How can I test my mic and hear myself?
faq.a: Open the mic test, allow microphone access, and record a clip of up to 10 seconds. Press Play to hear it. The clip is what the microphone picked up, so it shows how you sound to other people. The test does not play your voice back live.

faq.q: Can I hear myself live while I talk?
faq.a: Not in this tool. Mic Test records a clip and plays it back afterward. Live monitoring is usually a setting in your headset or audio app, so check there if you need your voice in your ears while you speak.

faq.q: Is it safe to record my voice in a mic test?
faq.a: The clip stays in your browser. Mic Test uploads nothing and saves nothing, and no account is needed. Close the page and the clip is gone. Use headphones and a quiet room for the cleanest check.

pages.claim: Open the mic test in Safari on your iPhone, tap Allow when it asks for the microphone, and talk: the meter moves when the mic picks up your voice. Record 10 seconds and play it back. Free, no app.

sections.heading: Test your iPhone mic in Safari
sections.body:
Open Safari and go to the [iPhone mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/iphone). When Safari asks to use the microphone, tap Allow.

1. Speak at normal volume and watch the meter move.
2. Tap record and speak for up to 10 seconds.
3. Stop the recording and tap play to hear it.

No app is needed. The test runs in Safari, so you open a page and allow the microphone. Nothing is installed.

sections.heading: If Safari does not ask for the microphone
sections.body:
If you tapped Don't Allow earlier, or no prompt appears, reload the page and look for the microphone prompt again. Then close Safari and open the page once more. Also check that no call app, voice recorder or video app is holding the microphone, because only one app can use it at a time in many cases.

For more on Safari on iPhone, Apple's guide is at [Customize your Safari settings](https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/customize-your-safari-settings-iphb3100d149/ios).

sections.heading: What the meter and playback tell you
sections.body:
The meter shows that sound is reaching the page. The playback shows how that sound is recorded. Listen for muffled or clipped words, a volume that drops out, and hiss or background noise.

Hold the phone the way you do on a call and record again. A hand or a phone case can cover the mic and make your voice sound thin or far away.

sections.heading: Using earbuds or a headset
sections.body:
If you use earbuds or a headset, look for it in the microphone list when more than one is shown. Pick it, record a short clip, and play it back. The clip tells you whether that mic sounds clear enough for calls.

**Test the same device you will use on the call.** A clip from the phone mic does not tell you how a headset mic will sound.

If you test often, keep the same setup each time: the same earbuds or headset, the same spot, and the same way of holding the phone. That makes the clips easy to compare. Record a new clip whenever you change something, and play back the newest one before you rely on it. A clip from last week tells you nothing about a headset you plugged in today. For a call on the phone, sit in a quiet room, keep the phone at the distance you use when you talk, and speak as you would on the call.

If the clip sounds fine but the meter barely moves, speak a little louder for the next take so you can see the level change. The meter shows that the mic is active, and the playback shows how your voice sounds.

faq.q: How do I test my mic on my iPhone?
faq.a: Open the mic test in Safari, tap Allow when the microphone prompt appears, and speak. The meter moves when the mic hears you. Record a clip of up to 10 seconds and play it back to hear how you sound.

faq.q: How do I know my mic is on my iPhone?
faq.a: If the meter moves while you talk, the iPhone mic is picking up sound in Safari. If it stays flat, the mic is not getting access or is in use by another app. Reload the page, allow the microphone again, and run the test once more.

faq.q: Does the iPhone mic test need an app?
faq.a: No. Mic Test runs in Safari, so you open a web page and allow the microphone. Nothing is installed and no account is needed. Nothing is uploaded or saved, and the recording goes away when you close the page.

pages.title: Mic Test for Zoom: Check Your Mic Before a Call | Lazur
pages.description: Check your mic before a Zoom call with a free browser test: a live meter and 10-second playback. Then confirm Zoom's own microphone test. No sign-up.
pages.claim: Run this mic test first: allow the mic, speak, and check that the meter moves and the playback sounds clear. Then open Zoom's own Test microphone button to confirm Zoom uses the same mic. Free, in your browser.

sections.heading: Check the mic here first
sections.body:
Start with the browser test. It shows whether the mic works and how loud it is.

1. Open the [mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/zoom) and select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone.
2. Pick the mic you will use on the call, if there are several.
3. Speak normally and check that the meter moves.
4. Record 10 seconds, then play it back.

This tells you the mic works and is loud enough. It does not tell you whether Zoom is using that same mic, so run Zoom's own check next.

sections.heading: Run Zoom's own microphone test
sections.body:
Zoom has a built-in test in the desktop app.

1. Open the Zoom desktop app and click your profile picture in the top-right corner.
2. Select Settings.
3. Open the Audio tab.
4. In the Microphone section, click Test microphone.
5. Watch the Input volume bar. It should move when Zoom picks up sound, and your recording plays back.

If the bar does not move, choose a different microphone from the menu, or adjust the input level. Zoom's help article is [Testing your audio settings for Zoom meetings](https://support.zoom.com/hc/en/article?id=zm_kb&sysparm_article=KB0062765).

sections.heading: If this test and Zoom disagree
sections.body:
The usual cause is the microphone. For example, Zoom might use your laptop mic while the browser test uses your headset. Set the same microphone in the Audio tab in Zoom, then run both checks again.

Close other apps that might hold the mic, such as another call app or a recorder, and test again. A clean result in both places is what you want before you join.

If you join calls from more than one place, run the check in each one. A desk, a kitchen and a car all sound different to a mic. When Zoom shows a different mic than you expected, go back to the Audio tab and choose the one you want before you join. Running both checks is quick, which is a small cost before a call that matters.

If Zoom's test works but the browser test does not, the browser permission is the likely cause. Allow the microphone for your browser, reload the page, and run the browser test again.

sections.heading: Before the meeting
sections.body:
Run both checks a few minutes before the call, from the same spot and with the same headset you will wear. Speak the way you will speak in the meeting, not in a whisper, so the level you see is realistic.

**A recording you can play back is the best check.** A meter alone does not show whether your voice sounds clear to other people.

faq.q: Why can't Zoom detect my microphone?
faq.a: Zoom usually cannot see a mic that is unplugged, blocked by another app, or not chosen in its settings. Check that the mic is connected, select it in Zoom's Audio tab under Microphone, and close other apps that use it. Then run Test microphone again.

faq.q: How do I test my mic in Zoom?
faq.a: Open Zoom's Settings, go to Audio, and click Test microphone under Microphone. Zoom records your voice and plays it back, and the Input volume bar moves when it hears you. If the bar does not move, choose a different mic.

faq.q: Can I test Zoom by myself?
faq.a: Yes. The Test microphone button records you and plays it back, so no one else needs to join. Zoom also has a test meeting you can join to preview your audio and video before a real call.

pages.description: Check your mic before a Discord voice chat with a free browser test: a live meter and 10-second playback. Then run Discord's own Mic Test. No sign-up.
pages.claim: Discord has its own Mic Test in the Voice & Video settings. Run this browser test first: allow the mic, watch the meter, and play back a 10-second clip. Free, no app, no sign-up, nothing uploaded.

sections.heading: Run the Discord mic test
sections.body:
Start with this browser test, then check Discord.

1. Open the [mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/discord) and select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone.
2. In Discord, open your settings and go to the Voice & Video tab.
3. Under Mic Test, click Let's Check.
4. Speak and watch Discord's input meter move.

Discord's Mic Test is available on the desktop app and in the browser, not on the phone app. Discord's help article is [Mic Testing](https://support.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/360020641332-Mic-Testing).

sections.heading: What each test checks
sections.body:
This tool shows you the level from your mic and lets you hear a recording of it. Discord's Mic Test shows how Discord hears you through the microphone it has selected. Use both. This page confirms the mic works and sounds clear. Discord's test confirms Discord is using that same mic.

If the two disagree, the mic Discord has selected is the likely reason, so check the input device in the Voice & Video tab.

sections.heading: If Discord does not pick up your voice
sections.body:
Check the input device in Discord's Voice & Video tab. Make sure it matches the mic that works in this browser test. Then look at the input volume and any other audio options on that tab, and run Let's Check again.

If nothing changes, close other apps that use the mic and restart Discord. Then run both tests again from the start.

sections.heading: Test before you join
sections.body:
Run both checks before you join a voice channel, using the same headset you will wear. The level meter shows that sound arrives. The playback here shows how you sound, which is what the other people in the channel will hear.

**Use the same device for both tests.** Switching mics between the browser check and Discord can make the two results disagree.

If you move between a headset and the built-in mic, check Discord after each change. The Voice & Video tab shows the device Discord uses, so look there first when the level from this browser test and Discord's own check do not match. Keep the window open while you speak during Let's Check, and say a full sentence so the meter has something to show. If you use a game overlay or another app that records audio, close it for the test, then open it again once the levels look right.

If Discord's meter still stays flat, choose a different microphone in Discord and compare the result with this browser test. A mic that works here but not in Discord points to Discord's own input setting. A mic that fails in both places points to the device or its connection, so try another cable, port or headset to check.

faq.q: How do I do a mic test on Discord?
faq.a: In Discord, open your settings, go to Voice & Video, and under Mic Test click Let's Check. Speak and watch the input meter. The test works on the desktop app and in the browser, not on the phone app.

faq.q: Is the mic test on Discord accurate?
faq.a: It shows how Discord hears the mic it has selected at that moment, so it is a good check of your setup. It is not a guarantee of how a call will sound. Pair it with a 10-second playback here to hear the clip yourself.

faq.q: How can I test my mic audio?
faq.a: Open this mic test, allow the microphone, and speak. The meter should move. Record up to 10 seconds, then play it back to hear your mic. If the meter does not move, pick another microphone in the list.

pages.title: Mic Test on Windows 11: Check Your Mic Free | Lazur
pages.description: Test your Windows 11 microphone in Settings, then check it in the browser with a live meter and 10-second playback. Free, no app or sign-up needed.
pages.claim: Open Settings, then System, then Sound. Under Input, pick your mic and select Start test to check it in Windows. Then run this browser test for a live meter and a 10-second playback. Free, no sign-up.

sections.heading: Test the mic in Windows 11
sections.body:
Microsoft's steps for Windows 11 are below.

1. Connect your microphone to your PC.
2. Select Start, then Settings, then System, then Sound.
3. In the Input section, select the microphone you want to test.
4. Select the arrow (>) to the right of the device to open its Properties page.
5. Under Input settings, select Start test. Speak at your normal volume.
6. Select Stop test, then choose Play to hear your recording.

If the level is low, adjust the Input volume slider on the same page. Microsoft's full guide is [How to set up and test microphones in Windows](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/hardware/drivers/how-to-set-up-and-test-microphones-in-windows).

sections.heading: Check it in the browser
sections.body:
Windows' test shows the mic inside Windows. The browser test shows what a website receives from the same mic. Open the [mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/windows), allow microphone access, and pick the mic if you have more than one. Watch the meter, record 10 seconds, and play it back.

If the two tests disagree, the browser may be using a different input. Choose the microphone again in the list and test again.

sections.heading: If the browser test shows nothing
sections.body:
Check that Windows uses the mic you picked in the Input section. Then make sure microphone access is allowed for apps and for your browser. Those settings are in Windows Settings under the microphone privacy options. Close any other app that might be using the mic, such as a call app, and test again.

If the meter stays flat in every app, the problem is most likely the device or its driver. Try another mic or a headset to find out.

sections.heading: Which microphone to pick
sections.body:
Windows may list a laptop mic, a headset and a webcam mic. Test each one you plan to use, and pick the one with the clearest playback. The mic you choose in the browser test applies to that test only. Windows still keeps its own default input for other apps.

If you use a USB mic, a headset with a cable or a Bluetooth headset, plug it in or turn it on before you open Settings, so it appears in the Input list. Bluetooth headsets often switch between a listening mode and a calling mode, and the calling mode is the one that uses the mic. Pick the headset in the Input section and run Start test to check that it is the one Windows is using. Then run the browser test to see the same device from the website side.

Keep the microphone you chose connected while you test, because unplugging it in the middle of a test can stop the meter.

faq.q: How do I test my mic in Windows 11?
faq.a: Select Start, then Settings, System, Sound. Under Input, select your mic, open its Properties, and choose Start test under Input settings. Speak, select Stop test, then choose Play to hear it. Microsoft's guide has the full steps.

faq.q: How do I check if my PC has a mic?
faq.a: Open Settings, then System, then Sound, and look under Input. If a microphone is listed, Windows can see it. Then run the browser mic test here: if the meter moves when you speak, the mic also works in the browser.

faq.q: Why is my mic not working on Windows 11?
faq.a: The common causes are the wrong microphone selected, microphone access blocked, or another app holding the mic. Check the Input section, allow microphone access for apps and your browser, close other apps, and test again.

pages.title: Mic Test With Speaker: Hear Your Mic Through Speakers | Lazur
pages.description: Test your mic and hear the playback through your speakers in one browser page. Record 10 seconds, play it back, and watch the level meter. Free, no sign-up.
pages.claim: Mic Test checks your microphone and plays your recording back through the speakers or headphones your computer is using. It does not play test tones or check each speaker, so use it for the mic and the playback.

sections.heading: What this test covers
sections.body:
Mic Test checks the mic. It shows a live level meter and the loudest level so far, and it records up to 10 seconds that you can play back. The playback goes through whatever speakers or headphones your computer is using, so you hear the mic and your output in one check.

It does not play test tones, and it does not check left and right speakers one at a time. For that, use a separate speaker test.

sections.heading: Test the mic and the speaker together
sections.body:
1. Open the [mic test](https://mic-test.lazur.app/speaker) and select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone.
2. Pick the microphone if you have several.
3. Record 10 seconds, speaking clearly.
4. Press Play. If you hear your voice clearly, the mic and your speakers are working together.

If the clip is clear, you have a working pair. If it is quiet, raise the input level in your sound settings and record again.

sections.heading: If the playback is silent
sections.body:
If the playback is silent but the meter moved, the problem is most likely the speaker or the output device. Check its volume, and check which device your computer is sending sound to. Then press Play again.

If the playback is silent and the meter never moved, go back to the microphone steps first, because nothing was recorded.

sections.heading: Speakers or headphones
sections.body:
With speakers, the mic can pick up the playback and repeat it, which sounds like echo. Use headphones for a clean check, or turn the speaker down while you record. Headphones also show you what you sound like through the ears you will use on a call.

If your speaker volume is low, the clip will sound quiet even when the mic is fine. Turn the speaker or headphone volume up partway, then play the clip again. If the clip is loud but the words are hard to follow, the mic may be too far away or covered. Test the two parts separately if you are not sure: first the mic meter, which shows the input, then the playback, which shows the output. If both look right, the mic and the speaker are working for this check, and you can move on to a call or a recording.

Keep the volume at a level that is comfortable to you, not at the maximum, so you can hear both the mic and the playback clearly. If the playback has a hum or buzz, unplug any charger or power adapter nearby and test again. Electrical interference can add noise to a recording, so the clip will show you whether it is still there.

faq.q: How do I test a mic and speaker together?
faq.a: Open the mic test, allow the microphone, record up to 10 seconds, and press Play. You hear the clip through your speakers or headphones, so one check covers both. For left and right channels, use a separate speaker test.

faq.q: Does the mic test play sound?
faq.a: Only your own recording. Mic Test does not play tones or test each speaker. The clip plays through the speakers or headphones your computer is using.

faq.q: How can I test my mic and hear myself?
faq.a: Record a clip in the mic test and play it back. You hear exactly what the mic captured. Wear headphones so the speaker does not send sound back into the mic.

pages.title: The Audio Track Is Paused on a Mic Test: Fix It | Lazur
pages.description: Your mic test says the audio track is paused and the meter does not move? Here is what that usually means and how to fix it, with a free browser check.
pages.h1: The audio track is paused mic test
pages.claim: A paused audio track usually means the browser is not getting sound from the microphone you picked. Choose the right mic, allow access, close apps that hold it, and run the test again. Free, no sign-up.

sections.heading: What the message usually means
sections.body:
This message usually means the browser is connected to a microphone but is not receiving sound from it right now. The page has no audio to show, so the meter stays flat.

The usual causes are a different mic selected than the one you are speaking into, the mic muted at the system level, another app holding the mic, or a device that was unplugged or disconnected after the page loaded.

sections.heading: Fix it in this mic test
sections.body:
1. Pick the microphone you want to test in the list, if there are several.
2. Select Allow when the browser asks for the microphone. If you blocked it earlier, allow it in your browser's site settings, then reload the page.
3. Close other apps that use the mic, such as a call app or a recorder.
4. Start the test again and speak. The meter should move.

If it moves, record 10 seconds and press Play to check the sound.

sections.heading: Fix it in Windows or on iPhone
sections.body:
On Windows 11, go to Settings, then System, then Sound, and check the Input section. Select the right mic and use Start test. The steps are on the [Windows page](https://mic-test.lazur.app/windows).

On an iPhone, the steps are on the [iPhone page](https://mic-test.lazur.app/iphone). Close any app that might be recording, then open the test in Safari and allow the microphone.

sections.heading: When the meter still does not move
sections.body:
Unplug the mic and plug it back in, or try another microphone or a headset. Restart the computer or phone if nothing changes. If the mic works in another app but not here, the browser may need permission again.

If the meter stays flat in every app, the problem is probably the device, its cable or its driver, and it needs checking or replacing.

If you see the message right after you open a page, reload the page once before you change anything else. If the message comes back after a reload, check the mic in your sound settings, because the browser can only use the input your computer provides. Then try the same mic in another app that records sound, such as a voice recorder. If that app records fine, the problem is more likely the browser's permission for the mic than the mic itself.

If the test works after you change the input in your sound settings, note that setting. Keep it selected for future calls, and check it again after you update your system or plug in a new device, since the default input can change when a device is added.

If the meter still does not move after all of these steps, write down what you tried and in what order. That list is useful if you contact the device maker or your computer's support team, because it shows which steps you have already ruled out.

faq.q: Why is my mic suddenly not working?
faq.a: A mic that stops working is usually held by another app, muted at the system level, or switched to a different device. Close other apps that use the mic, check the input in your sound settings, then reconnect the mic and test again.

faq.q: What does the audio track is paused mean?
faq.a: It usually means the browser has a microphone connected but is not getting sound from it. Choose the right microphone, allow access, close other apps, and run the test again. If the meter stays flat in every app, the device needs checking.

faq.q: How do I fix my mic audio?
faq.a: Start with the input. Select the right microphone, raise the input volume in your sound settings, and keep the mic close while you speak. Record a 10-second clip and play it back to hear the change.
